steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on adding interactive visualizations to Sprite, a system for building computer vision models from video, to help users find images where models make mistakes. Situate it in interactive machine learning and teaching, describe what we built and the usability study, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Background: interactive ML and machine teaching, its stages and their challenges
- What this paper does: augmentation to Sprite for planning and evaluation
- Usability study and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - interactive ML and teaching: reduce complexity of building ML models with a human in the loop
  - loop stages: curriculum building, knowledge transfer, model evaluation
  - simple to define, but challenging
  - curriculum building: unknowns (unseen examples, features model is blind to), bias
  - knowledge transfer: limited to inputs a learning algorithm permits; hard for teachers to express rich knowledge
  - model evaluation: related to explainable ML (XAI)
  - system can only give feedback and confidence about what it knows
- This paper
  - augmentation to Sprite: train CV models applied to images from video footage
  - focus: planning and evaluation stages
  - support subject domain experts (task knowledge, not necessarily ML expertise): find challenging documents (images) where model performs poorly, and why
  - user and learning system collaborate through interactive visualizations to find images to label and add to training set
  - two views: timeline view, scatterplot view
- Study and contributions
  - usability study: how views help participants identify (evaluate) and select (plan) images the model struggles on
  - two conditions: baseline (Sprite without augmentation) vs visualization (with augmentation)
  - contribution 1: visualizations for sampling images with diverse prediction errors (Section 3); browse/find candidates; compare prediction behavior of one or more models (classification, object detection)
  - contribution 2: study results: participants more efficient at finding candidate images that stumped the model vs baseline
  - contribution 3: insights, design implications, future directions for subject-domain experts in interactive machine teaching of CV models

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Research in interactive Machine Learning (ML) and teaching  has made progress in making it less complex to create ML models, by having a human in the loop. This interactive loop can be described in terms of curriculum building, knowledge transfer, and model evaluation stages. Defining these teaching tasks is in principle straightforward, but it has challenges. For curriculum building, unknowns (e.g., examples the model has not seen or features the ML model is blind to) and bias are obstacles that can get in the way of the task. Knowledge transfer can be limited to the inputs that a learning algorithm allows, and there are still challenges in letting teachers in the loop express rich knowledge. Model evaluation is an activity directly related to topics in explainable ML (XAI). In an interactive ML model-building process, the system can only give feedback and confidence about what it knows.

In this paper we describe an augmentation to Sprite, which lets users train CV models that are applied to images that come from video footage. Sprite is a system to build CV models from video footage. We focus on the planning and evaluation stages. We want to support subject domain experts (people who have knowledge relevant to the task the model is doing, and who do not necessarily have ML expertise) in efficiently finding challenging documents (images) where the model does not perform well, and also in finding the potential reasons why. Our enhancement supports users with these challenges by improving the interactive machine teaching process, so that the user and the learning system work together through interactive visualizations to find images that should be labeled (and added to the training dataset) to improve the CV model. We propose two interactive visualizations in Sprite, a timeline view and a scatterplot view.

We ran a usability study to assess the effects of the interactive visualizations. The study looked at how our views, the timeline and scatterplot views, help participants identify (evaluate) and select (plan) images where a model is struggling to make correct predictions. We tested two conditions: baseline (Sprite without our augmentation) and visualization (Sprite with our augmentation). With this assessment our work makes the following contributions. First, we designed interactive visualizations and studied how they can help users who are training CV models to more efficiently sample images that contain diverse prediction errors in the context of Sprite (see Section 3). The visualizations support users in browsing and finding candidate images and in assessing and contrasting the prediction behavior of one or more models (e.g., classification and object-detection models). Second, we present results of a study showing that participants using these interactive visualizations were more efficient at finding candidate images that stumped the model than with the baseline condition. Finally, we give insights, discuss design implications, and suggest future directions for supporting subject-domain experts during interactive machine teaching of CV models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Research in the field of interactive Machine Learning (ML) and teaching [1,2] has made progress in reducing the complexity of creating ML models by putting a human in the loop [3,1,4,5]. This interactive loop can be characterized by curriculum building, knowledge transfer, and model evaluation stages [2]. While defining these teaching tasks is in principle straightforward, it presents challenges. In curriculum building, the existence of unknowns (e.g., examples a model has not seen or features an ML model is blind to) and the presence of bias are obstacles that can get in the way of the task [6]. The transfer of knowledge can be limited to the inputs a learning algorithm permits, and challenges persist in allowing teachers in the loop to express rich knowledge [7,8]. Model evaluation has a direct relationship with topics in explainable ML (XAI) [9,10]. In an interactive ML model-building process, the system can only provide feedback and confidence about what it knows.

This paper describes an augmentation to Sprite that allows users to train CV models that are applied to images originating from video footage. We focus on the planning and evaluation stages, seeking ways to support subject domain experts (people with knowledge germane to the task the model is performing, who do not necessarily have ML expertise) not only in efficiently identifying challenging documents (images) in which the model is not performing well but also in identifying the potential reasons why. Our enhancement supports users facing these challenges by improving the interactive machine teaching process, so that a user and the learning system collaborate through interactive visualizations to find images that should be labeled (and added to the training dataset) to improve the CV model. We propose two interactive visualizations, a timeline view and a scatterplot view, in the context of Sprite, a system to build CV models from video footage.

We conducted a usability study to assess the effects of these interactive visualizations. The study examined how our views (the timeline and scatterplot views) help participants identify (evaluate) and select (plan) images about which a model struggles to make correct predictions. We tested two conditions: baseline (Sprite without our augmentation) and visualization (Sprite with our augmentation). With this assessment, our work offers the following contributions. First, we have designed interactive visualizations and studied how they can help users who are training CV models more efficiently sample images that contain diverse prediction errors in the context of Sprite (see Section 3). These visualizations support users in browsing and finding candidate images and in assessing and contrasting the prediction behavior of one or more models (e.g., classification and object-detection models). Second, we present the results of a study showing that participants using these interactive visualizations were more efficient at finding candidate images that stumped the model than when using the baseline condition. Finally, we provide insights, discuss design implications, and suggest future directions for supporting subject-domain experts during interactive machine teaching of CV models.
